questions.stem: Which is the most common method of data-at-rest encryption on Windows workstations, especially valuable for lost or stolen removable media?
questions.explanation: Full disk encryption (BitLocker on Windows) protects data at rest; if an encrypted drive is lost you only lose hardware, not data.
questions.trap: A screensaver password locks an unattended session but does nothing if the drive itself is removed and read elsewhere.

questions.stem: A strong password is described as having high entropy. Which set of attributes achieves that?

choices.text: Short, memorable, reused across sites, never changed
Length, complexity, uniqueness, and regular expiration
The same word with a number appended each month

questions.explanation: High entropy comes from length (8+ characters), complexity (mixed character types), uniqueness (no reuse), and regular expiration (e.g. every 30-90 days).
questions.trap: Reusing a short memorable password across sites is exactly what produces low entropy and high risk.

questions.stem: Which BIOS/UEFI password prevents changes to the firmware settings themselves?
questions.explanation: A supervisor password prevents changes to the firmware settings. A user/boot password stops the computer from starting until entered.
questions.trap: The user/boot password gates startup, not the firmware settings menu; that is the supervisor password's job.

questions.stem: A user in an open office handles PII on screen. Which two end-user practices best reduce shoulder-surfing risk?

choices.text: Use a privacy filter and shield the screen when entering passwords
Share one login among the team

questions.explanation: Privacy filters block side viewing and shielding the screen when typing passwords defends against shoulder surfers near sensitive data.
questions.trap: Disabling the firewall weakens security and is unrelated to shoulder surfing.

questions.stem: What is the recommended tool for managing many unique, complex passwords?

choices.text: A sticky note under the keyboard
A password manager (an encrypted vault secured by a master password)
Storing them in a plain-text file on the desktop

questions.explanation: A password manager is an encrypted vault for all credentials, secured by a single master password, so each site can have a unique complex password.
questions.trap: Reusing one password everywhere defeats uniqueness; a breach of one site then exposes all of them.

questions.stem: For temporary contract staff, which account-management control ensures their access is automatically revoked when their contract ends?
questions.explanation: Setting an account expiration date automatically revokes access when a temporary worker's contract ends.
questions.trap: Login-time restrictions limit WHEN someone can log in, not WHETHER the account expires.

questions.stem: An account freezes after too many incorrect password attempts. Which control is this, and what does it defend against?

choices.text: Account expiration; defends against stale accounts
Least privilege; defends against privilege creep

questions.explanation: A failed-attempts lockout freezes an account after too many wrong tries, frustrating brute-force and guessing attacks.
questions.trap: Account expiration deals with end-of-term access, not repeated wrong-password attempts.

questions.stem: When setting up a brand-new device, which hardening step does the review say to do immediately?

choices.text: Change the default administrator account and password

questions.explanation: Attackers have lists of default credentials, so change the default administrator account and password the moment you set up a new device.
questions.trap: Enabling AutoRun and the guest account both increase attack surface - the opposite of hardening.

questions.stem: Why does the review recommend disabling AutoRun on modern Windows?

choices.text: It speeds up the boot process
It is a dangerous legacy feature that automatically ran programs from USB drives
It prevents Windows Update from running

questions.explanation: AutoRun automatically executed programs from inserted USB drives - a dangerous legacy behavior, which is why it is disabled in modern Windows.
questions.trap: AutoRun is a security risk, not a boot-speed feature; disabling it reduces attack surface.

questions.stem: To reduce the attack surface of a workstation, what should you do with Windows services that aren't being used?

choices.text: Leave them running in case they're needed later
Set them all to automatic start
Move them to a different drive

questions.explanation: Every background service is a potential vulnerability, so disable any services that are not being used to reduce attack surface.
questions.trap: Leaving unused services running keeps unnecessary entry points open - the opposite of hardening.
